title: Trump to Announce $700 Million Coal Revival, Invoking Cold War-Era Law
summary:
President Donald Trump is again reaching into the past to try to revive the future of coal. On Thursday, he is expected to announce a nearly $700 million investment to support coal-fired power plants and coal exports, invoking a Cold War-era national defense law to justify the spending.

The plan, outlined by a White House official, would use authority under the 1950 Defense Production Act to aid 13 coal plants across the country and help construct new ones in Alaska and West Virginia — which would be the first new U.S. coal plants since 2013. The funds would also restart a coal-fired plant in Maryland and support a long-delayed coal export terminal in Oakland, California. Together, the administration says, the moves will support or create more than 14,000 jobs in coal, construction, rail, and maritime industries.

Trump is expected to be joined by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Energy Secretary Chris Wright, and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin for the announcement. It’s the latest in a series of pro-coal actions: last fall, the administration opened 13 million acres of federal lands for coal mining and provided $625 million to recommission or modernize coal plants. Trump also issued executive orders early in his term to keep aging fossil-fuel plants running past their retirement dates, citing rising electricity demand from data centers, artificial intelligence, and electric vehicles.

Energy Secretary Wright has argued that emergency orders to keep coal and gas plants operating helped prevent major blackouts during a severe cold snap in late January and early February.

But environmental groups are pushing back hard. “Propping up coal billionaires with taxpayer money is one more way for the Trump administration to put polluters first and put the rest of us at risk,” said Kit Kennedy, managing director for power at the Natural Resources Defense Council. She added that the plan would lead to higher electricity bills and dirtier air, quipping, “What’s next, a taxpayer bailout to build new phone booths?”

Coal, once the dominant source of U.S. electricity at over 50%, fell to about 15% in 2024, undercut by cheaper natural gas and the growth of renewables. U.S. coal exports also dipped during Trump’s second term, partly due to Chinese tariffs. Global coal demand hit record levels recently but is expected to flatten or decline.

Critics say the best path for the climate and consumers is to let uneconomic coal plants retire peacefully. But for now, the administration is betting hundreds of millions of dollars that coal still has a future.
why_it_matters: The decision to spend hundreds of millions of dollars on coal affects the air you breathe, the climate you will inherit, and the kind of energy that will power your home and school in the coming decades — making this a direct fight over the country's energy future.

background_read: The Defense Production Act of 1950, signed during the Korean War, gives the president broad powers to direct industrial production for national defense; it has been used for everything from steel production to vaccine manufacturing during the COVID-19 pandemic.

President Donald Trump (the U.S. president since 2025) has long promised to bring back coal jobs, even as the market shifted toward cheaper natural gas and rapidly growing solar and wind power, making coal generation uneconomic in many places.

The Natural Resources Defense Council (a large U.S. nonprofit environmental advocacy group) has successfully challenged several previous Trump-era rules that aimed to roll back pollution limits, often in court.

China, one of the world's biggest coal buyers, imposed tariffs on U.S. coal during Trump's second term, cutting into American exports and complicating any attempt to revive the industry through foreign sales.
Global coal demand reached record highs in recent years, but international agencies project it will plateau or decline as more countries switch to cleaner energy to meet climate goals.

└─ officials: Interior Secretary Burgum, Energy Secretary Wright, and EPA Administrator Zeldin will join him.

└─ jobs claim: Over 14,000 jobs in coal, construction, rail, and maritime industries.

└─ justification: Soaring electricity demand from data centers, AI, and electric vehicles used as a reason to keep plants running.

perspectives.description: Supporters argue coal provides reliable, always‑available electricity that can prevent blackouts during extreme weather. The investment could save thousands of jobs in mining communities and strengthen national energy security, especially when foreign supply chains are uncertain.

Environmental groups see this as a taxpayer-funded gift to a dying, polluting industry that will increase health problems and greenhouse gas emissions. They point out that natural gas and renewables are cheaper now, so propping up coal will lead to higher bills for families and businesses.

Using the Defense Production Act for coal is an unorthodox move; historically it was used to boost military production or critical supply chains like medical gear. The policy reflects a wider global struggle over how much governments should intervene in energy markets to preserve legacy industries versus letting them adapt or fail.

If the plan moves ahead, it may face lawsuits challenging the use of the Defense Production Act for non-defense purposes. Over the next few years, the new coal plants' viability will depend heavily on government subsidies and whether international coal demand keeps slipping, so the experiment could either become a model of industrial revival or a costly dead end.
